FastAPI gives you multiple tools to enrich your OpenAPI schema — from individual path parameters to request body fields. Here's a complete breakdown:

---

## 1. 📍 Adding Metadata to Path Parameters with `Path()`

You use the `Path` class (imported from `fastapi`) along with `Annotated` to declare metadata for path parameters.

### Step 1: Import `Path` and `Annotated`

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, Path, Query
```

`Path` is imported directly from `fastapi`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-params-numeric-validations/]

### Step 2: Declare `title` and other metadata

You can declare all the same parameters as for `Query`, such as `title` and `description`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-params-numeric-validations/]

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, Path, Query

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_items(
    item_id: Annotated[int, Path(title="The ID of the item to get")],
    q: Annotated[str | None, Query(alias="item-query")] = None,
):
    results = {"item_id": item_id}
    if q:
        results.update({"q": q})
    return results
```

> **Note:** A path parameter is always required as it has to be part of the path. Even if you declared it with `None` or set a default value, it would not affect anything — it would still be always required. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-params-numeric-validations/]

### Available metadata & numeric validation parameters for `Path()`

With `Query`, `Path`, and others you can declare metadata and string validations in the same ways. You can also declare numeric validations: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-params-numeric-validations/]

| Parameter | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| `title` | A title for the parameter |
| `description` | A description for the parameter |
| `alias` | An alias name |
| `deprecated` | Mark as deprecated |
| `gt` | Greater than |
| `ge` | Greater than or equal |
| `lt` | Less than |
| `le` | Less than or equal |

```python
):

```

```python
from fastapi import Body, FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI()

    price: float = Field(gt=0, description="The price must be greater than zero")
```

question: How can I stream a list of items with FastAPI while also using a dependency to manage query parameters for filtering the items?
answer:
I now have all the information needed to give a comprehensive answer. Here's a complete guide:

---

## Streaming a List of Items with a Dependency for Query Parameter Filtering

This combines two powerful FastAPI features:
1. **Stream JSON Lines** — using `yield` in a path operation function to stream items one by one.
2. **Dependency Injection** — using a class or function as a dependency to cleanly manage and validate query filter parameters.

---

### How Each Piece Works

#### 1. Streaming Items with `yield`

Instead of using `return` in your path operation function, you use `yield` to produce each item in turn. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/stream-json-lines/]

"Streaming" means your app starts sending data items to the client without waiting for the entire sequence to be ready. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/stream-json-lines/]

FastAPI will send each item as a **JSON Lines** response (`application/jsonl`), where each JSON object is on its own line. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/stream-json-lines/]

If you declare a return type (e.g., `AsyncIterable[Item]`), FastAPI will use it to **validate**, **document**, **filter**, and **serialize** the data using Pydantic — and you get much higher performance thanks to Pydantic's Rust-based serialization. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/stream-json-lines/]

#### 2. Dependency for Query Parameters

You can declare a **class as a dependency** whose `__init__` parameters become the query parameters. FastAPI will parse, validate, and inject them automatically. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/classes-as-dependencies/]

Alternatively, you can use a **Pydantic model** with `Query()` to group related query parameters, reuse them across endpoints, and declare validations all at once. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-param-models/]

---

### Full Example

```python
from collections.abc import AsyncIterable
from typing import Annotated, Literal

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Query
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI()


# --- Pydantic model for filter query parameters ---
class FilterParams(BaseModel):
    limit: int = Field(100, gt=0, le=100)
    offset: int = Field(0, ge=0)
    order_by: Literal["name", "description"] = "name"
    search: str | None = None


# --- All items in our "database" ---
class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str | None


all_items = [
    Item(name="Plumbus", description="A multi-purpose household device."),
    Item(name="Portal Gun", description="A portal opening device."),
    Item(name="Meeseeks Box", description="A box that summons a Meeseeks."),
    Item(name="Microverse Battery", description="Powers the whole ship."),
    Item(name="Fleeb", description=None),
]


# --- Streaming path operation using the dependency ---
@app.get("/items/stream")
async def stream_items(
    filters: Annotated[FilterParams, Query()]  # Dependency injected via Query()
) -> AsyncIterable[Item]:
    # Apply filtering
    results = all_items
    if filters.search:
        results = [i for i in results if filters.search.lower() in i.name.lower()]

    # Apply ordering
    results = sorted(results, key=lambda i: getattr(i, filters.order_by) or "")

    # Apply pagination
    results = results[filters.offset : filters.offset + filters.limit]

    # Stream each item one by one
    for item in results:
        yield item
```

---

### How It All Fits Together

| Concept | How it's used |
|---|---|
| `yield` instead of `return` | Streams each `Item` to the client as it's produced [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/stream-json-lines/] |
| `AsyncIterable[Item]` return type | Enables Pydantic validation, serialization, and OpenAPI docs [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/stream-json-lines/] |
| `FilterParams(BaseModel)` | Groups all query params into a reusable, validated Pydantic model [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-param-models/] |
| `Annotated[FilterParams, Query()]` | Tells FastAPI to extract each field from the query string [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-param-models/] |
| `Field(100, gt=0, le=100)` | Adds validation constraints directly on the model fields [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-param-models/] |

---

### Example Request

```
GET /items/stream?search=portal&limit=10&offset=0&order_by=name
```

FastAPI will:
1. Parse and validate the query parameters into a `FilterParams` instance.
2. Inject it into `stream_items` via the dependency system.
3. Stream back matching `Item` objects as JSON Lines, one per line.

---

### Tips

- You can also use a **class-based dependency** with `Depends()` instead of `Query()` if you prefer more control or need to share logic across many endpoints. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/classes-as-dependencies/]
- You can add `model_config = {"extra": "forbid"}` to your `FilterParams` model to reject any unexpected query parameters with a clear error. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-param-models/]
- For non-async functions, use `Iterable[Item]` as the return type instead of `AsyncIterable[Item]` — FastAPI will ensure it doesn't block the event loop. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/stream-json-lines/]

**"Dependency Injection"** means, in programming, that there is a way for your code (in this case, your *path operation functions*) to declare things that it requires to work and use: "dependencies".

question: How can I implement a FastAPI endpoint that changes the response status based on certain conditions and also checks for a fixed query parameter value using a dependency?
answer:
To implement a FastAPI endpoint that dynamically changes the response status based on certain conditions and checks for a fixed query parameter value using a dependency, you can follow these steps:

1. **Create a Dependency for Query Parameter Validation**:
   Define a dependency that checks for a specific query parameter value.

2. **Modify the Endpoint to Change the Response Status**:
   Use the `Response` object to set the status code based on conditions within the endpoint logic.

### Example Code

Here's an example code snippet illustrating these concepts:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response, Depends, status
from typing import Annotated

app = FastAPI()

# Dependency to check for fixed query parameter value
def validate_query(param: str | None = None):
    if param != "expected_value":
        raise ValueError("Invalid query parameter value.")
    return param

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_item(
    response: Response,
    param: Annotated[str | None, Depends(validate_query)] = None
):
    if param == "expected_value":
        # Return 200 status if condition is met
        response.status_code = status.HTTP_200_OK
        return {"item": "This is your item with the expected query parameter."}
    else:
        # Return 404 if condition is not met
        response.status_code = status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND
        return {"error": "Item not found."}
```

### Explanation:

1. **Dependency Function**:
   - The `validate_query` function checks the `param` query parameter. It raises a `ValueError` if the value is not as expected. FastAPI handles this exception and returns a 422 Unprocessable Entity response automatically.

2. **Endpoint Logic**:
   - The endpoint `/items/` receives the `Response` object and the validated query parameter `param`.
   - If the `param` matches the expected value, it sets the response status to 200.
   - If not, it sets the status to 404.

You can customize the success and error messages as needed. This basic structure helps build endpoints that respond dynamically based on input conditions while maintaining clean validation via dependencies.

question: What utility does Pydantic provide for handling settings from environment variables?
answer:
Pydantic provides a powerful utility called **Pydantic Settings** (`pydantic-settings`) for handling settings and configurations from environment variables. Here's a comprehensive overview:

---

## Pydantic Settings for Environment Variables

### What It Is

Pydantic provides a great utility to handle settings coming from environment variables through **[Pydantic: Settings management](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/pydantic_settings/)**. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/settings/]

---

### Installation

You need to install the `pydantic-settings` package separately: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/settings/]

```console
$ pip install pydantic-settings
```

It also comes included when you install FastAPI with all extras: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/settings/]

```console
$ pip install "fastapi[all]"
```

---

### How It Works

You import `BaseSettings` from `pydantic_settings` and create a subclass, very much like a regular Pydantic model. You declare class attributes with type annotations and optional default values. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/settings/]

```python
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    app_name: str = "Awesome API"
    admin_email: str
    items_per_user: int = 50
```

When you create an instance of the `Settings` class, Pydantic will **read environment variables in a case-insensitive way** — so an upper-case variable `APP_NAME` will still be read for the attribute `app_name`. It will then **convert and validate the data**, so `items_per_user` will be an `int`, for example. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/settings/]

---

### Key Features

1. **All Pydantic validation features** — You can use all the same validation tools you use for Pydantic models, like different data types and additional validations with `Field()`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/settings/]

2. **`.env` file support** — If you have many settings that change across environments, you can put them in a `.env` (dotenv) file and Pydantic Settings will read them as if they were environment variables. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/settings/]

   ```python
   from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

   class Settings(BaseSettings):
       app_name: str = "Awesome API"
       admin_email: str
       items_per_user: int = 50

       model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env")
   ```
   [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/settings/]

3. **Dependency injection support** — You can provide settings via a FastAPI dependency, which makes it very easy to override settings during testing. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/settings/]

4. **Caching with `@lru_cache`** — Using `@lru_cache` lets you avoid reading the dotenv file again and again for each request, while still allowing you to override it during testing. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/settings/]

---

### Running with Environment Variables

You can pass configurations as environment variables when running the server:


question: Why do we need to use `Union` instead of the vertical bar for the `response_model` argument in FastAPI even in Python 3.10?
answer:
In FastAPI, even with Python 3.10, you need to use `Union` instead of the vertical bar (`|`) for the `response_model` argument. This is because when passing types to arguments, such as `response_model`, Python interprets the vertical bar as an operation rather than as a type annotation. Here’s a breakdown of the reasoning:

1. The vertical bar is valid in type annotations (e.g., `some_variable: PlaneItem | CarItem`), but when you use it in an assignment like `response_model=PlaneItem | CarItem`, Python tries to perform an invalid operation between `PlaneItem` and `CarItem` instead of recognizing it as a type declaration for FastAPI. [source_url](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/extra-models/)

2. Therefore, when defining the `response_model`, you must use `Union` to indicate that the response can be one of the specified types. This ensures that FastAPI processes it correctly within its framework for validation and response generation. [source_url](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/extra-models/)

In summary, while Python 3.10 allows using the vertical bar for typing, it cannot be used in all contexts where types are defined as function arguments. Instead, `Union` must be employed for parameters like `response_model` in FastAPI.

---

## Multiple Body Parameters + OAuth2 Authentication in FastAPI

The two features are combined cleanly using FastAPI's **Dependency Injection** system. Here's a full breakdown:

---

### 🔑 Part 1: OAuth2 Authentication Setup

FastAPI provides `OAuth2PasswordBearer` from `fastapi.security` to implement OAuth2 with the Password flow using a Bearer token. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/security/first-steps/]

You create an instance of it by passing the `tokenUrl` — the URL the client will use to send credentials and get a token: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/security/first-steps/]

```python
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")
```

You then build a `get_current_user` dependency that receives the token via `Depends(oauth2_scheme)`, decodes and validates it (using JWT), and returns the authenticated user. If the token is invalid, it raises an HTTP 401 error immediately. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/security/oauth2-jwt/]

You can also chain a `get_current_active_user` dependency on top of `get_current_user` to additionally check that the user is not disabled. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/security/oauth2-jwt/]

---

### 📦 Part 2: Multiple Body Parameters

You can add multiple body parameters to a path operation function by declaring multiple Pydantic model parameters. FastAPI will notice there is more than one body parameter and automatically use the parameter names as keys in the expected JSON body. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-multiple-params/]

For example, with `item: Item` and `user: User`, FastAPI expects:
```json
{
    "item": { "name": "Foo", "price": 42.0 },
    "user": { "username": "dave" }
}
```
[https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-multiple-params/]

You can also add **singular values** as body fields using `Body()`, otherwise FastAPI would treat them as query parameters: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-multiple-params/]

```python
importance: Annotated[int, Body()]
```

---

### 🔗 Part 3: Combining Both — Full Example

Here is a complete working example that combines multiple body parameters with OAuth2 JWT authentication:

```python

from typing import Annotated

import jwt
from fastapi import Body, Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer, OAuth2PasswordRequestForm
from jwt.exceptions import InvalidTokenError
from pwdlib import PasswordHash
from pydantic import BaseModel

# --- Config ---
SECRET_KEY = "your-secret-key-here"  # use: openssl rand -hex 32
ALGORITHM = "HS256"
ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 30

app = FastAPI()

# --- Security Setup ---
oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")
password_hash = PasswordHash.recommended()

# --- Fake DB ---
fake_users_db = {
    "johndoe": {
        "username": "johndoe",
        "full_name": "John Doe",
        "email": "johndoe@example.com",
        "hashed_password": password_hash.hash("secret"),
        "disabled": False,
    }
}

# --- Pydantic Models ---

class Token(BaseModel):
    access_token: str
    token_type: str

class TokenData(BaseModel):
    username: str | None = None

class User(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str | None = None
    full_name: str | None = None
    disabled: bool | None = None

class UserInDB(User):
    hashed_password: str

# --- Body Models for the secured endpoint ---
class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str | None = None
    price: float
    tax: float | None = None

class OrderUser(BaseModel):
    username: str
    full_name: str | None = None

# --- Auth Helpers ---

def get_user(db, username: str):
    if username in db:
        return UserInDB(**db[username])

def authenticate_user(db, username: str, password: str):

    if not user or not password_hash.verify(password, user.hashed_password):

    return user
```

# Implementing User Authentication with Jinja2 Templates in FastAPI

You can combine both features in your FastAPI application. Here's how each part works:

## Setting Up Jinja2 Templates

You can use any template engine you want with FastAPI, and a common choice is Jinja2. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/templates/]

To use Jinja2 templates, you need to:
1. Import `Jinja2Templates` from `fastapi.templating` [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/reference/templating/]

```python
from fastapi.templating import Jinja2Templates

templates = Jinja2Templates(directory="templates")

@app.get("/items/{id}", response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def read_item(request: Request, id: str):
    return templates.TemplateResponse(
        request=request, name="item.html", context={"id": id}
    )
```
[https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/templates/]

## Setting Up User Authentication

FastAPI supports all the security schemes defined in OpenAPI, including HTTP Basic, **OAuth2 with JWT tokens**, and API keys in headers, query parameters, or cookies. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/features/]

For a robust authentication system using OAuth2 with JWT tokens, you would:

1. Use `OAuth2PasswordBearer` and `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` for handling credentials [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/security/oauth2-jwt/]
2. Use `pwdlib` for password hashing and verification [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/security/oauth2-jwt/]
3. Use `PyJWT` to create and decode JWT tokens [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/security/oauth2-jwt/]

```python

    to_encode.update({"exp": expire})
```

```python
async def dashboard(
    request: Request,
    current_user: Annotated[User, Depends(get_current_active_user)]
):
    return templates.TemplateResponse(
        request=request, name="dashboard.html", context={"user": current_user}
    )
```

FastAPI doesn't make any compromise with any database, data model, or tool — it gives you all the flexibility to choose the ones that fit your project best, and you can use well-maintained packages like `pwdlib` and `PyJWT` without any complex integration mechanisms. question: How can multiple processes communicate on the same port and IP address in FastAPI deployments?
answer:
To enable multiple processes to communicate on the same port and IP address in FastAPI deployments, you typically utilize a load balancer. This is particularly effective when you deploy your FastAPI application within container management systems like Kubernetes. Here's how it works:

1. **Single Load Balancer**: You can configure a single load balancer that listens on the main port (e.g., 8000) and distributes incoming requests to multiple worker processes or containers running identical instances of your FastAPI app. This allows you to handle more requests simultaneously by utilizing multiple processes or containers running your application [source](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/).

2. **Replication of Workers**: In a typical setup, each container runs a single instance of the FastAPI application (i.e., a process) and operates independently in memory. The load balancer takes care of distributing the incoming traffic across all available worker containers, ensuring that requests are handled in a balanced manner [source](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/) [source](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/concepts/).

3. **Internal Networking**: Container orchestration tools manage the internal networking so that the load balancer can communicate with the individual containers effectively. Requests are routed through the load balancer to the appropriate container based on the load balancing algorithm used [source](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/).

In summary, using a load balancer to manage multiple worker processes or containers allows your FastAPI application to handle requests on the same port and IP address efficiently.

question: What are the deployment options for a FastAPI application in a Docker container that can also utilize multiple Uvicorn workers for better performance?
answer:
Here is a comprehensive breakdown of all the deployment options for a FastAPI application in Docker, including how and when to use multiple Uvicorn workers:

---

## 🐳 FastAPI in Docker: Deployment Options with Uvicorn Workers

### 1. The Standard Dockerfile (Single Process)

The most common and recommended starting point is building a Docker image from the official Python base image. A standard `Dockerfile` looks like this:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.14

WORKDIR /code

COPY ./requirements.txt /code/requirements.txt

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade -r /code/requirements.txt

COPY ./app /code/app

CMD ["fastapi", "run", "app/main.py", "--port", "80"]
```

This runs a **single Uvicorn process** inside the container. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

> ⚠️ **Always use the exec form** of `CMD` (i.e., `CMD ["fastapi", ...]`) — never the shell form (`CMD fastapi ...`). The exec form ensures FastAPI can shut down gracefully and that lifespan events are triggered properly. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

---

### 2. Deploying the Container Image

After building the image, there are several ways to deploy it: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

- **Docker Compose** on a single server
- **Kubernetes** cluster
- **Docker Swarm Mode** cluster
- **Other tools** like Nomad
- **Cloud services** that run container images for you

---

### 3. Replication Strategies: Where to Handle Multiple Workers

This is the core decision point. There are **two main strategies**:

---

#### ✅ Strategy A: One Process per Container (Recommended for Clusters)

When using a distributed container management system like **Kubernetes**, **Docker Swarm**, or **Nomad**, you should handle replication **at the cluster level**, not inside the container. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

- Run a **single Uvicorn process per container**, but spin up **multiple containers**.
- A **load balancer** (which may also act as a TLS Termination Proxy) distributes incoming requests across the containers. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]
- Each container is identical, running the same app, but with its own process and memory — enabling true parallelization across CPU cores or even different machines. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

> In this case, you **would NOT** want to use `--workers` inside the container. Adding a process manager inside the container would only add **unnecessary complexity** that your cluster system is already handling. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

**Memory benefit:** Running a single process per container gives you a well-defined, stable, and limited memory footprint per container, making it easier for Kubernetes to schedule containers across machines. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

---

#### ✅ Strategy B: Multiple Workers Inside a Single Container (Special Cases)

There are valid scenarios where you **do** want multiple Uvicorn workers inside a single container. You can enable this with the `--workers` flag in your `CMD`: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.14

WORKDIR /code

COPY ./requirements.txt /code/requirements.txt

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade -r /code/requirements.txt

COPY ./app /code/app

CMD ["fastapi", "run", "app/main.py", "--port", "80", "--workers", "4"]
```

You can also use the `uvicorn` command directly: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/server-workers/]

```bash
uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --workers 4
```

**When does this make sense?**

- **Simple App on a Single Server:** Your application is simple enough to run on a single server (not a cluster), and you want to take advantage of multiple CPU cores. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]
- **Docker Compose:** You're deploying to a single server with Docker Compose, where managing replication of multiple containers with shared networking and load balancing is not straightforward. In this case, a single container with multiple worker processes is a practical solution. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

> ⚠️ **Memory Warning:** If you run multiple processes per container, make sure the total number of processes doesn't consume more memory than what is available on the host. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

---

### 4. The Deprecated Base Image (Don't Use)

There used to be an official FastAPI Docker image (`tiangolo/uvicorn-gunicorn-fastapi`) that bundled Gunicorn to manage Uvicorn workers. **This image is now deprecated** and you should not use it. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

> The image was created when Uvicorn didn't support managing and restarting dead workers, so Gunicorn was needed. Now that Uvicorn (and the `fastapi` command) support `--workers` natively, there's no reason to use that base image. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]

---

### 5. Summary Decision Table

| Scenario | Recommended Approach |
|---|---|
| Kubernetes / Docker Swarm / Nomad | Single Uvicorn process per container, replicate at cluster level |
| Single server with Docker Compose | Single container with `--workers N` |
| Simple single-server app | Single container with `--workers N` |
| Cloud service managing replication | Single Uvicorn process per container |

The key takeaway: **none of these are rules written in stone**. You should evaluate your own use case and decide what best covers your deployment needs around HTTPS, startup, restarts, replication, memory, and pre-start steps. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker/]
